title: Human Skeletal & Cardiovascular System Facts
answer: An adult human skeleton consists of exactly 206 bones, with the Femur (thigh bone) being the largest and strongest, and the Stapes (in the middle ear) being the smallest. The ABO blood group system (discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1900) classifies blood into A, B, AB, and O: O-negative is the universal red blood cell donor, and AB-positive is the universal recipient.
highlights: Skeletal Count: 206 bones in adult (infants are born with ~270 bones which fuse over time)
Largest & Smallest Bones: Largest/Strongest = Femur; Smallest = Stapes (stirrup bone in ear, ~3 mm)
Blood Groups: Discovered by Karl Landsteiner (1930 Nobel Prize); O-Negative (O-) is universal donor (lacks A, B, and Rh antigens); AB-Positive (AB+) is universal recipient
Normal Blood Pressure: 120/80 mmHg (120 mmHg Systolic / 80 mmHg Diastolic measured with a Sphygmomanometer)

title: Common Infectious Diseases, Pathogens & Vectors
answer: Malaria is caused by the protozoan parasite Plasmodium (P. falciparum) transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Dengue is a viral infection caused by Dengue virus transmitted by day-biting Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Tuberculosis (TB) is an airborne bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, preventable with the BCG vaccine.
highlights: Malaria: Protozoan parasite (Plasmodium falciparum / vivax); Vector: Female Anopheles mosquito; Treatment: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), Quinine
Dengue Fever (Breakbone Fever): Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes aegypti; causes severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count drop) and hemorrhagic risk
Tuberculosis (TB): Bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis; attacks lungs; diagnosed via Mantoux test and Sputum microscopy; treated via DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course)
Typhoid: Bacterium Salmonella typhi transmitted via contaminated food/water; diagnosed with Widal Test
Cholera: Bacterium Vibrio cholerae producing severe acute watery diarrhea; managed with Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)

title: Vitamins, Physiological Roles & Deficiency Diseases Reference
answer: Vitamins are organic micronutrients essential for metabolism: Vitamin A (Retinol — deficiency causes Night Blindness / Xerophthalmia), Vitamin B1 (Thiamine — deficiency causes Beriberi), Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid — deficiency causes Scurvy), and Vitamin D (Calciferol — deficiency causes Rickets in children and Osteomalacia in adults).
highlights: Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K): Vitamin A (Retinol — vision/immunity; Night Blindness), Vitamin D (Calciferol — bone health/calcium; Rickets), Vitamin E (Tocopherol — antioxidant; neurological issues), Vitamin K (Phylloquinone — blood clotting factor synthesis; hemorrhagic bleeding)

Water-Soluble Vitamins (B-complex, C): Vitamin B1 (Thiamine — Beriberi), Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin — Cheilosis), Vitamin B3 (Niacin — Pellagra: 4Ds), Vitamin B9 (Folic Acid — Megaloblastic anemia & neural tube birth defects), Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin — Pernicious anemia)
Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid): Synthesizes collagen, aids iron absorption; deficiency causes Scurvy (spongy bleeding gums, impaired wound healing)

title: Human Immune System: Innate, Adaptive Immunity & Vaccines
answer: The immune system defends the body against pathogens via Innate Immunity (non-specific, rapid: skin, stomach acid, phagocytes) and Adaptive/Acquired Immunity (pathogen-specific with immunological memory). B-lymphocytes produce antibodies for humoral immunity, while T-lymphocytes (Helper CD4+ and Cytotoxic CD8+) mediate cell-mediated immunity.
highlights: B-Cells (Humoral Immunity): Mature in bone marrow; differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antigen-specific Immunoglobulins / Antibodies (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD)
T-Cells (Cell-Mediated Immunity): Mature in the Thymus gland; Helper T-cells (CD4+) activate B-cells and macrophages; Cytotoxic T-cells (CD8+) destroy virus-infected and cancerous cells

Active vs Passive Immunity: Active immunity is generated by the host's own immune system upon infection or vaccination (long-lasting memory); Passive immunity is the direct transfer of pre-formed antibodies (e.g., mother's colostrum containing IgA, anti-venom; short-term protection)

title: Nutrition Caloric Values & Body Mass Index (BMI) Formula
answer: Body Mass Index (BMI) evaluates body fat based on height and weight: BMI = Weight (kg) / [Height (m)]². The energy values of macronutrients are: Carbohydrates yield 4 kcal/g, Proteins yield 4 kcal/g, and Fats/Lipids yield 9 kcal/g.
highlights: BMI Formula: BMI = Weight in kg / (Height in metres)²
WHO BMI Classifications: Underweight (< 18.5), Normal Weight (18.5 – 24.9), Overweight (25.0 – 29.9), Obese Class I (30.0 – 34.9), Obese Class II (35.0 – 39.9), Morbidly Obese (≥ 40.0)
Macronutrient Energy Density: Carbohydrates (4 kcal/g / 17 kJ/g), Proteins (4 kcal/g / 17 kJ/g), Fats (9 kcal/g / 37 kJ/g), Alcohol (7 kcal/g)
Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR): Minimal rate of energy expenditure required to sustain vital involuntary body functions at rest

title: Human Blood Pressure — Normal Ranges and Physiology
answer: Normal resting blood pressure for a healthy adult is approximately 120/80 mmHg (Systolic 120 mmHg during ventricular contraction / Diastolic 80 mmHg during ventricular relaxation). Measured using a Sphygmomanometer and stethoscope. Hypertension is diagnosed when blood pressure consistently exceeds 140/90 mmHg (or 130/80 mmHg under AHA guidelines).
highlights: Systolic pressure: Maximum pressure in arteries during ventricular systole (~120 mmHg)
Diastolic pressure: Minimum pressure in arteries during ventricular diastole (~80 mmHg)
Pulse pressure = Systolic - Diastolic (normal ~40 mmHg)
Hypertension stages: Stage 1 (130-139 / 80-89 mmHg), Stage 2 (≥140 / ≥90 mmHg), Hypertensive crisis (>180 / >120 mmHg)
Cardiac output = Heart rate (72 bpm) × Stroke volume (70 mL) ≈ 5.0 Litres/min

title: Human Endocrine System — Glands and Hormones
answer: The endocrine system secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream. Key glands: Pituitary (Master gland at base of brain, secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, Oxytocin, Vasopressin), Thyroid (Thyroxine T₄ and Triiodothyronine T₃ regulating basal metabolic rate), Pancreas (Insulin from β-cells lowers blood sugar; Glucagon from α-cells raises blood sugar), Adrenal (Adrenaline/Epinephrine for fight-or-flight; Cortisol for stress), Pineal (Melatonin for sleep-wake circadian rhythm).
highlights: Pituitary gland: Called master gland; controlled by Hypothalamus via releasing hormones
Pancreatic Islets of Langerhans: Beta cells secrete Insulin; Alpha cells secrete Glucagon
Diabetes mellitus: Type 1 (autoimmune destruction of β-cells); Type 2 (insulin resistance and secretory defect)
Thyroid gland requires Iodine to synthesize Thyroxine; deficiency causes Goitre
Adrenal medulla secretes Adrenaline (emergency hormone increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and glycogen breakdown)

title: Human Immune System — Innate & Adaptive Immunity (B & T Cells)
answer: The human immune system provides dual defense: (1) Innate Immunity (non-specific, immediate defense: skin physical barrier, stomach acid chemical barrier, neutrophils, macrophages, complement system), and (2) Adaptive Immunity (antigen-specific, creates long-term immunological memory): Humoral Immunity mediated by B cells producing Antibodies (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD) and Cell-Mediated Immunity mediated by T cells (CD4+ Helper T cells activating responses and CD8+ Cytotoxic T cells destroying virus-infected/cancer cells).
highlights: B Lymphocytes (mature in Bone marrow): Differentiate into Plasma cells (secreting thousands of antibodies/sec) and Memory B cells
T Lymphocytes (mature in Thymus): CD4+ T-Helper cells direct immune response (target of HIV virus); CD8+ Cytotoxic T-cells trigger apoptosis in infected cells via perforin and granzymes

Antibody classes: IgG (most abundant 80%, crosses placenta), IgM (first responder, pentamer), IgA (in secretions: tears, saliva, breast milk), IgE (allergic reactions and parasites), IgD (B-cell receptor)
Active Immunity (induced by infection or vaccines with memory) vs Passive Immunity (preformed antibodies: anti-venom, mother's colostrum)

title: Insulin, Glucagon & Diabetes Mellitus Physiology
answer: Blood glucose homeostasis is maintained by pancreatic Islets of Langerhans: Beta (β) cells secrete Insulin to facilitate cellular glucose uptake via GLUT-4 transporters and promote glycogenesis in liver/muscle; Alpha (α) cells secrete Glucagon to stimulate glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis during fasting. Type 1 Diabetes is an autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells (absolute insulin deficiency); Type 2 Diabetes is characterized by peripheral insulin resistance and progressive secretory defect.
highlights: Normal Fasting Blood Sugar: 70–99 mg/dL (Prediabetes: 100–125 mg/dL; Diabetes: ≥126 mg/dL)
Postprandial (2-hour after meal) Blood Sugar: <140 mg/dL (Diabetes: ≥200 mg/dL)
HbA1c (Glycated Hemoglobin): Reflects average blood sugar over past 3 months; Normal <5.7%, Prediabetes 5.7–6.4%, Diabetes ≥6.5%

Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): Life-threatening complication primarily in Type 1 where extreme insulin absence forces fatty acid breakdown into acidic ketone bodies (acetone, acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate)
Metformin: First-line oral drug for Type 2 diabetes that inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK activation
